content: Pertussis, also known as whooping cough, is an acute and prolonged infectious respiratory illness caused by Bordetella pertussis, a fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus. This disease can lead to significant morbidity, particularly in adolescents and adults whose immunity from childhood vaccination or prior infection has waned and who have not received booster immunization with the Tdap vaccine (tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis). In 2004, women aged 15–39 years accounted for 97% of all live births in the United States. Between 2000 and 2006, 103,940 cases of pertussis were reported to the CDC's National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), with 27% of these cases occurring in individuals aged 15–39 years. Parents, including new mothers, are a significant source of B. pertussis transmission to infants, particularly during early infancy when the risk of complications and fatalities is highest. Infants under 12 months of age accounted for 93% of pertussis-related deaths reported to the CDC during this period. The introduction of decennial booster vaccination with the Td vaccine (tetanus and reduced diphtheria toxoids) has significantly reduced the annual number of tetanus and diphtheria cases. However, the average annual number of pertussis cases during the same period remained high at 14,849. In 2005, two Tdap vaccines were licensed in the United States: Adacel® for individuals aged 11–64 years and Boostrix® for those aged 10–18 years. Both vaccines are approved for single-dose administration. No vaccine containing acellular pertussis antigens without tetanus and diphtheria toxoids is available in the United States. Vaccinating adolescents and adults with Tdap reduces the burden of pertussis among vaccine recipients and may prevent transmission to infants. The CDC's Advisory Committee for Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends routine Tdap vaccination for women of childbearing age during routine health assessments before conception to prevent pertussis morbidity during pregnancy. Additionally, Tdap is recommended for adults and adolescents who anticipate contact with infants under 12 months of age to reduce the risk of transmission. In 2006, ACIP recommended routine administration of Tdap for postpartum women who had not previously been vaccinated with Tdap to provide personal protection and reduce the risk of transmitting pertussis to their infants. However, the safety and efficacy of Tdap use during pregnancy have not been demonstrated, and it is not recommended for pregnant women in any country. There is no evidence that Tdap administered during pregnancy harms the fetus or increases the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Additionally, the protective effect of transplacental maternal antibodies induced by Tdap on infants has not been established. Pertussis is highly infectious, with attack rates among exposed, non-immune household contacts as high as 80–90%. The most infectious periods are the catarrhal and early paroxysmal phases. Untreated patients, particularly infants, can remain infectious for six weeks or longer. Among older children and adults with prior vaccination or infection, the infectious period is typically less than 21 days. Infants under 12 months of age are at the highest risk for severe pertussis, often requiring hospitalization for respiratory or other complications. The risk of death or severe pertussis is highest in the first six months of life and remains elevated until infants receive at least one or two doses of the pediatric DTaP vaccine. Complications and deaths from infant pertussis are often associated with necrotizing bronchiolitis, primary or secondary pneumonia, and co-infections with bacterial and viral pathogens. Pulmonary hypertension has also been increasingly recognized among fatal infant cases. Parents, particularly mothers, are the most common source of pertussis transmission to infants. Approximately 75% of pertussis cases among infants under six months of age with an identified source are linked to household contacts. Vaccination of household contacts and close relatives, including parents, can significantly reduce the risk of pertussis transmission to infants. The diagnosis of pertussis is complicated by the limitations of currently available diagnostic tests. Culture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are the only tests accepted for confirming pertussis cases for national reporting purposes. Culture is 100% specific but has variable sensitivity, ranging from 30–60% early in the disease course. PCR offers increased sensitivity and faster turnaround times but is affected by specimen collection techniques and laboratory variability. Postexposure prophylaxis and treatment of pertussis typically involve macrolide antibiotics such as erythromycin, azithromycin, or clarithromycin. Early antimicrobial treatment during the catarrhal phase can modify the severity of symptoms and reduce transmission risk. However, treatment initiated later in the disease course generally does not alter symptom severity but can still prevent further transmission.
